blocks.x: Interview with Milton Baptiste, February 5th, 1997, real number one. Okay. I wanted to give me your full name.
Milton Joseph Baptiste, Jr.
Okay. You know, I had some questions about Baptiste. Do you all spell it with one T?
No, no, no. With two T's.
You spell Baptiste with two T's?
Yeah, B-A-T-I-S-T-E.
Okay.

The other T is B-A-T-T-I-S-T-E. There's not that many families that spell it like that here. But there is another family that's B-A-P-T-I-S-T-E. That's Baptiste. That is the original way of spelling it. The way my name is spelled is like the material.
Okay.

You see, the families came along through the years when they wanted to be distinguished from that Baptiste family to that Baptiste family to the other Baptiste family. And they started adding things in like two T's, one P, no P, and so forth. To say that that was that family from there and that family from there. But we're all Baptistes.
Okay. So you're all originally B-A-P?
Yeah. That's the original spelling of the family name. B-A-P-T-I-S-T-E.
Okay.
So it was changing along the line. Harold Baptiste and I spelled the name the same way.
He spelled it with two T's. Yeah. How old is it? How old is it?
He's a person. He's a three T.
Well, B-A-T-T.
I-S-T-E is three T's.
Right. Let me see.
I spell it with two T's.
Right. B-A-T.
I-S-T-E.
But are you and Harold related? Or would you?
We really don't know.
Okay.
Who can say that out of the city of New Orleans where there's, I know of 35 Baptistes.
Okay.
And we all play music.
The 35 that you know?
There's 35 people I know.
Just off the top of my head, Alvin, you related to Alvin?
Well, we don't. That's what I'm saying. We can't really sing.
And Earl? There's Earl.
There's Earl Baptiste. Quentin. Earl Quentin Baptiste who's gone. There's Alvin Baptiste. There's Harold Baptiste. There's Lionel Baptiste. There's the whole Baptiste brothers family.
Right.

Okay. And then, oh, there's some other, okay, Earl Baptiste's father played banjo. His name was Baptiste also. There's a Henry Baptiste back in the days that played bass. And, man, oh, I guess we could go on and on. Baptiste's a big family of musicians. Generically, we must be related somewhere. Okay. Or somehow.
Now, what was your father's name?
My father's name was Milton Baptiste.
Okay. So you're a junior? I'm junior.
Yeah.
Okay.
But my father didn't play music. He tinkled one finger on the piano. That's all he'd do. I'd do. But his father, I was told, was a Jamaican bass player.
Ah, okay. And what was his name?
I can't remember. He never really revealed his father's name. Would you be surprised?
Okay. Now, when your father died, in the obituary, it says that his mother's name was Elizabeth Paul and Scipio, Baptiste Scipio. Okay. Now I remember. S-C-I-P-I-O.
Now I remember. Now I remember. Now I remember. Now I remember. His father's name was Scipio.
Scipio. Okay. Scipio.
The same second name as my brother.
Ah, okay.
My brother's name is Maurice Scipio. So, now I remember. We are. Okay. After all, I'm 62 now. The mind is getting a little laxed.
That happens. I can't remember stuff. I'll tell you.
I can't remember the last tune I played on the last gig. What are you talking about? That was only Sunday.
So, your grandfather, you know stories about your grandfather, Scipio?

My daddy never told me many stories about him. Only the fact that he said he was a bass player. A bass, in those days they'd call it a bass violin. Bass violin, yeah. Yeah, but I never had that many stories. Now, on my father's side, I had an aunt. Her name was Felicia Boykins. And she actually raised my father. Okay. Felicia was also a lead singer in the choir at the Sixth Union Baptist Church. She was a gospel singer.
Okay.

And I can remember when I was really young because my family was Catholic and Baptist. Father's side was Baptist. Mother's side was Catholic. And my daddy was a convert to the Catholic religion. Okay. But my aunt, who raised him, she was a staunch gospel singer at this church. I think it was Reverend Dennis had that church on Arlene Street across from the project. And she was a lead singer. She organized a choir and all that. And I remember her telling me when I was really younger because I would be playing Ritim and Blues on the street or whatever and so forth. She'd say, play that gospel. Let's get into gospel. She'd say, that's all right. Wait till you get older. You're going to find out.
Right.
And she would know she was right.
And you'd have more appreciation.
Oh, I have lots more appreciation because the jazz and the gospel are so closely related.
Yeah.
You can't do one without the other.
Right. Yeah.

And it's the basic foundation for all the other musics that have come from that era. Right. Yeah. So it's a lot of relationships is so closer to me now as an older person than it was when I was Ritim and Blues and running on the road by G. Clark and Shirley and Lee Witherspoon and Jimmy Liggins and all that when I was a teenager.
Right.
Yeah.
So I didn't get your birthday. Can you tell me your birthday?
September 5th, 1934.
1934. So your September what?
Five.
Five.
Yeah.
Okay. So in your mother's name, give me your mother's name.
My mother's name is Mary Batiste.
All right.
Her maiden name was Jolivet.
Jolivet. Yeah. Okay. And could you tell me? Actually, I've got a story.
J-O-L-I-V-E-T-T-E.
E. Okay.
Uh-huh. But actually, Mary was her second name. She had one of those good old Creole Felicia. Uh, Feliciana.
Uh-huh.
Was her first name.
All right.
Yeah.
Feliciana Mary.
Feliciana Mary.
Jolivet.
No, no. Yeah, Jolivet.
Yeah. Jolivet. Okay. Yeah. Was your father from New Orleans? Did he grow up here?
Well, as far as I know, most of my father's life was here, but he came from like across the river in Mandeville, Madisonville, around that area.
Okay. Across the lake.
Across the lake. I'm sorry.
Yeah.
Across the lake. Yeah. Where there are a lot of a community of Batiste families. Oh, yeah.
Oh.
Okay. Right over there. Interesting. Yeah. So, and part of his origin, like I said, Scipio, his father, and his father and so forth, were Jamaicans.
Jamaicans. Yeah. Okay. Yeah. And so you don't know much about that side?
I don't.
And your mother's side? Now, how far back can you trace that?
Now, my mother's side, we can go back as far as my grandmother, who was a part Indian, part of the Blackfoot tribe. And she was a slave in Brobridge on the Edwards farm.
All right.

And that probably is the reason why her maiden name was Virginia Edwards. Okay. And then she married my grandfather, who was an interpreter in World War I. And he, actually he's an African, French African, because he interpreted English, you know, French English for generals in the First World War. And then he came to America and so forth, back in the earlier days, before that.
Right.
And my grandmother was married, gee, in the 1800s something, I don't know about that name.
And what was your grandfather's name?
His name was Joseph Charles Jolivet. Okay.
And your grandmother's name? Virginia Edwards.
Virginia Edwards. Yeah.

Yeah. Yeah, Edward seems to be a fairly common name in that area. Yeah. In South Leeds, from like St. James, I've known St. John's and St. Charles. Yeah, and that's where she's from, Brobreak. And in South Leeds, it seems to be a very big clan.
Well, it was a big clan because they had a large plantation.
Yeah.
And they had a lot of slaves. All the slaves took on the names of the slave owners, evidently. My grandma was cousin to Governor Edwards.
Look, given Louisiana, given Louisiana, look, you never know.
Well, his grandparents won't mind.
Hey, that's very possible. How many brothers and sisters did you have? Did you have a big family, I think?
My mother had 12 children.
That's a lot.

And I am the first. In between my brother, who's living now, there's two brothers, and up until yesterday I had six sisters. I only have five now. One of my sisters we parried yesterday. And there was eight of us from my mother. Six girls and two boys.
Can you give me a, can you list them? Can you give me a?
Well, it's easy. All names begin with M.
Oh, really? They name this?

Okay. As a matter of fact, this comes from the top. My father's name was Milton. My mother's name was Mary. Okay. The first born was me, Milton. Okay. The next is Maurice. The next is Merlene. The next is Mary. The next was Miriam. The next is Martha. Miriam. Okay.
And Mercedes.
All right.
Did they do that on purpose obviously? What's there?
My father must do it on purpose. Yeah, on purpose?
Sure. I was going to say.
My first wife was named Myrtle. Oh God.
Your first wife was named Myrtle.
And my brother broke that up. His wife, his name was Annetta. Oh. But my wife now is named Ruby.
My mother was named Myrtle. Okay. So you, okay where did you grow up? Where were you on?

Oh I grew up in the Samoa, in the melting pot of musicians. Okay. I was born in 1623 Columbus Street. Okay. And that's right around the corner from the Burbank's and the Telus Falls and the Peters and the Jean-Jean-Me Hall where the brass bands met and the Artesian Hall where the brass bands met. It was about three blocks from the Autocrat where it was the main black community's dance hall if you were light-skinned in Creole. And so I was born in a melting pot of musicians. As a matter of fact down the street from me lived the Pernell Brothers, about five doors away. I had music all around me when I was a kid.
Didn't the McLeans live in that? Like Richard?
Like Richard or Ernest McLean and so forth. They lived just a little, if I can remember they lived in the Six Ward on the other side of Esplanade Street.
And did Harold Deshawn live in that neighborhood?
Harold lived in the Southern Water, I'd say yeah. Somewhere around the Neck or St. Anthony or somewhere when he was a younger man.
I was wondering if you had contact with him as a kid. I didn't know.

I had contact with him as a kid but didn't know it. Because his sister and my mother were great friends and his sister ran a cleaning shop on Saint Bernard Street Street near Claybond. And when I would come home from school I would go to his sister's house to stay until my mother and father came home from work, you know, in those early days. He had came, he must have visited his sister at one time or another, but I didn't know because his nephew was named Gene Jackson. And Gene Jackson was my very best friend in the grammar school and so forth. I went to his house every evening to play for a while before going home knowing that my mother and father would get home from work.
So you all intersected at that point? But we didn't know. Years later you all went.
Oh many years later. 1950, oh gee, 1956.
That was the first time you'd worked with Harold?

That's the first time I met him in 1956. I heard about him, seen him on the street and so forth. But at that time I was traveling on the road with different road bands, rhythm and blues bands at the time. Sherilyn Lee, Lil Walter, Jimmy Reed. We used to work out of a local office here in New Orleans, Stovall, Percy Stovall was involved in booking bands and so forth. And so naturally we went out on gigs, you know, from Shaw, a booking agency out of New York. Milt Shaw was the guy who was doing all the big time R&B booking at the time. So we, that's what I was doing. And then my father, one day, this is 1960, but I would say.
And I had met Harold before, like I said about 56, and Ernie Caglietti I think.
Cag?
Yeah, a little Cag. I had to be operated on, take his leg off.
Oh okay, that's when he got his leg amputated.

So he couldn't do, because he was the trumpet player with Harold when he was in reorganization, around 55, 56, after getting some advice from Barry Martin from England. He told him, Duke you ought to reorganize the band that you played with as a kid, when he was 16 years old he played with the Olympia Serenaders, the original Olympia brass band. So he is an original member, who incidentally yesterday, on February the 4th, made 88 years old.
Was he that Duke at home?

Yes, yes. Yesterday he was 88 years old. He said, so he did, he organized, he started organizing a band with Anderson Minor, Andrew Anderson, Andrew Jefferson, Henry Glass, Kitschikola, George, you know.
What a lineup.

Yeah, and Manuel Powell, Paul Crawford. There was another guy, his name was Jim something. Oh no, we had, well sometime Chicken Hendry and Oscar would come over and play with us, and William Brown on tuba and so forth. These are the earlier people who I saw and I came into the band with, you know.
How, Dejon wanted you in the band?

Dejon wanted me because, well naturally, K couldn't walk anymore. Sure. So I took his place in the band. First gig I played was a gig at Anderson Minor. In those days you know, all these band leaders together, you get the job, we play your job as Olympia, because we're all together. So Anderson Minor had a practice parade for the Lions Club up in the uptown area. And they called me out that Sunday to do a practice parade. I said, you know, practice what?
Yeah, practice what's that? I mean, you're gonna practice music going, we just stick to the way of the hall.
Yeah. No, but it was practicing how to walk, drink, and play at the same time.
Walk, drink, and play at the same time.

Of course, that's what a practice parade is all about. You go from bar to bar, and go from each of the bar rooms in the local area that you're gonna be doing that Mardi Gras morning, you understand? Uh-huh. And then there's food, and there's drink, and you walk, and you play, and you walk. It's just like the same, it's a rehearsal for the day, you know. So they call it a practice parade.
How do you have a make it to the real thing, though?
I mean- Oh, when you get to the real thing, oh boy, that's it there. Much like the practice, just a little longer. It was enjoyable, though. So how were you-
Maybe jumping ahead, how were you accepted by the members of-
By the older guys?
Yeah, I mean, you coming from what I suspect was more of a R&B, rock and roll kind of background. Yeah, yeah.

I was met with a lot of opposition. I was met with a lot of opposition on, hey, come in and play in that rhythm and blues in the street. They don't want that rhythm and blues in the street. But what you gotta look at is, when I came along and so forth and so on, there was Young Pickett, also John Brunus Senior, who was with the Tuxedo Brass Band, and Andrew Morgan and those guys. And they had, just about the same time as I introduced Second Line to Olympia, Shirley Lee's song and the rhythm and blues feel was, Come on, baby, let the good time roll. Let the good time roll. So Tuxedo recorded that on Atlantic. Come on, baby, let the good time roll. So this was a help from us and from them to the young musician that there is a time change. There is a time of music. Bring new songs. You're bringing in new songs because you got new people walking and parading. Yeah. So the era of 1959 to 1965 became a transition area of rhythm and blues songs turned into traditional because they are traditional. Sure. These people have made these songs in the 50s and the 40s. This is 97. That's traditional. Right. What's traditional to me was not traditional to Kid Thomas. Mm-hmm. Because Kid Thomas were people who made songs from the 1800s. Sure. And so forth. And he changed them around. Sure. Kid Howard was the most progressive trumpet player of his era. Really? Of his time.
I never thought of Kid Howard as well.

Yeah, Kid Howard, man. And these guys, they were ahead of their time in music. Uh-huh. You know? Because some of the licks and some of the things that they play right now, hey, Wynton's only playing it faster.
Uh-huh.
Yeah. Okay. You know? And say, for instance, back in when I was 18, 19, 20, my idol was Wallace Davenport and Emory Thompson.
Uh-huh.
That was the Terence Blanchett and the Wynton Marsalis of today. Okay. Really. Yeah.
Those were the guys you were listening to? Oh, yeah. On. And where were you hearing them? In the street?

I heard mostly. No, no, not in the street. I didn't hear them in the street. Uh-huh. The guys I heard in the street was Percy Humphrey, Kid Thomas. Yeah. And, uh, oh, let's see. I have to, I have to, I have to, I can't, some of these older trumpet players, I can't remember their names. Right, right. You know? But they're, you know, like, uh, Don, uh, Don Albert. Sure. We went to town and played a lot of time. And, uh, we call him Piggy. Uh, John Albert. John Albert was, uh, was his name. Barak. We called him Barak. Right. And, you know, you had Jack Willis and all these.
Okay, yeah.
And, uh, all these people, uh, in other fields that I heard and so forth. And, uh, it made, it made for, oh, for many years.
What attracted you to the trumpet? What was the, the attraction?

Uh, I was about 11 years old. And I saw a movie at the Circle Theater. And it was a little colored boy laying on top of a dog's house playing the trumpet. Now don't ask me what movie and what. But that is the image that is still in my mind 50 years later here now. To decide, hey, if he could do it, I could. My mother sent me to Xavier University for 25 cents of lessons for piano. But in those days if you played the violin or the piano, it was a sissy. You know what I mean?
Oh, okay.

And a mama's boy. Right. So you didn't want to be a mama's boy. He wanted something, I wanted something rough. I wanted something to play. Yeah, man. I wanted to blast out. So, and I went to show this one Sunday and saw this little kid on top of a, I don't know what movie that was. But that is the funniest thing. And then I went to my parents. Did you actually take a few lessons on the piano? Yes, yes. Oh, I had to. Okay. Yeah.
No. So did you learn like the rudiments of music from the piano? No.

I really didn't learn much about the piano as I know now. And I don't know that very much about the piano now. Except I know card changes, I hear card changes, see card changes, and I can spell it out on the piano and so forth. But my mind was a blank to learn the piano because of what the guy said, hey he's a sissy playing that piano, or the violin. I wish I had played both of them. You know? So that was a blank to me. That didn't, that really didn't help me. It hindered me a lot. Because I would have a better knowledge even today of music.
If you'd really studied piano.
Yes, yes, yes. I advise all young musicians to grab a whole musical education in any and every instrument
possible. Because one instrument helps you with the other.

One will keep the other one enlightened. Yeah, definitely. You can be so, and piano is one of the basic instruments, the chord changes. Any rhythm instrument, guitar, violin, piano, any instrument that you have to learn, the chord changes, definitely to play or to execute the instrument at all, you should be, as a young musician, interested in. And take great interest, because it will help you much later. Say for instance if you decide to play for 50 years.
Yeah, yeah. Which I don't know, when you started you didn't know you were going to be playing for 50 years. I didn't know. No, no.
No I didn't know if I was going to be living for 50 years. Yes, right.
Well how much did you get all these other kids in your family, how much music was there in the household? Nobody.

Of all those kids? Of all my sisters and brothers, they had instruments they took up and put down. Right. My brother picked up the drums and put them down. Right. I have a sister who played the clarinet and left it on the bus. And that was it?
Yeah, well you know that's the extent.

Now some of them like to sing, you know. Right. I don't know where they can sing but I hope they just keep to their nursing and hairdressing jobs. It will be much better. But nobody at my deceased I imagine, they won't have any musicians following. Maybe my granddaughter has decided that she would like to play the clarinet. The Phoenicia, Phoenicia Matthews is her name. Maybe, maybe I'll have somebody coming out behind me.
Well there's a point, not a digression, the clarinet, I'm looking at a lot of the young bands today, Rebirth and you know the young kids coming out but I don't see any clarinet players.
There are very few clarinet players.
I don't see any clarinet players.

Again we get back, I haven't said anything about this but there is that element of musicians who learn and educate themselves and there's that element of young musicians now who go out to have a good time. And they learn up to a certain amount and that's it. They are not enough. And maybe, maybe, maybe, maybe I'm wrong about saying this but as up until five years or six years ago there wasn't enough serious musicians in this city, young musicians. But since Harold Batiste and Alice Marcel has returned to the city and put this jazz programs on the UNO and so forth, so they have found some of the cream of the crop of young musicians who really want to learn to be musicians and not just horn players on the street. And they want to improvise and enhance their musical abilities.
And have a real professional attitude about it.

That's right, that's right. That was the difference in a lot of brass bands too. There were those brass bands that could read, they read. You had to, when you were, when I was a young man, first getting with Harold Dejan and so forth, so they would give us music to read. With no titles on it or nothing. They just said number 31. Well I have to know that, after I got it into my head I knew 31 was a funeral march. And a very popular one that you played on the street. And they'd pass out music to the men, you see. Eureka, Olympia, Tuxedo, and let's see, I can't think of it.
Onward?
Oh yeah, Onward. And then there was the Excelsior. Excelsior. Yeah, yeah. These were the brass bands of my young era. And when you saw them on the street, you saw them with music.
Right.

Yeah, there were many marches and things that we played. And we had to read them, and read them correctly, because they were corrected parts or so forth. I'm sorry to say now, that a lot of the brass bands that's on the street now, they play in a 1-3-5 riff, and that's it. And they play it over, and they play it overly, disgustingly, overly, overly. The next number is the same damn thing. You know? And they're just not listening to the older musicians and things that have been handed down to them. The reason for me, we have just recorded a new CD, it's called Jazz Preservation List. On there are two of our inspiring contemporary jazz people, Donald Harrison Jr., Terrence Blanchett. Right. They wanted, especially to record with us, to record some of the old traditional tunes with a mixture of them and us, and us playing it in the old vein. And that's the new CD that we have out today. Cool. Cool stuff

so maybe some of these youngsters will listen at us play because they follow us they follow us in the wrong way they can follow us in the right way some of them have followers in the right way because we have other CDs and things that we recorded earlier in the 50s and 60s 60s and 70s before we really got down to recording and we do try I do try to keep that traditional good musicianship thing parts and so forth organization within the compounds of a brass band but some of the young sisters tell me and they play from two to three o'clock one number the baseline is the same boop which says nothing musically which says nothing that when he's 35 and 40 years old and his generation has changed and it will change to a more subtle music he won't know what to do do you
think I'm looking at this in the big picture could this just be generational ballyhoo I mean every generation complains about the next generation
sure they do sure they do
about the younger generation

sure they do they complain about us coming into the ranks yeah they complain about me bringing in rhythm and blues blah blah blah but rhythm and blues had its specific changes because what we were learning rhythm and blues changes from were some of our jazz greats you be blake and all those kind of people you know uh jellarone martin so forth that's where our rhythm and blues changes come from because uh in the 50s they were real this changes yeah it's just not the same change over and over and then what we were doing we were mixing that in with standard tunes okay yeah the standards is is known uh as traditional standard traditionals and we still play them today and the youngsters still think that it's uh oh that's old shit yeah but they can't play okay
all right reel number two with uh milton batiste february the 5th 1997 okay uh so when when you when you got with uh dejon John, were you a good reader? Could you read? I mean, were you adequate?
Well, I read music in high school and so forth, you know. Yeah, we had to. Unfortunately, I have a sight impairment. I was blind, blind in my right eye.
Oh, you're blind in your right eye? I'm blind. From birth?

From birth. I know nothing different than to see out of one eye. Okay. This pulls the difficulty, even as a young person. I was not accepted in the Army or the Navy because of that problem and because of the unfortunate accident, having to have hit in the head with a baseball when I was earlier, much earlier, younger, I want to say 11 years old maybe, and being an operator on for cancer of the scalp. So this gave me a lot of difficulties in reading the music. You understand? You have to look at music and you look straight across with peripheral vision. I don't have peripheral vision. I had to turn my head so forth. It's kind of difficult turning with the horn and getting the horn out of the way. Well, anyhow, I'll make a long story short. I was a poor reader. But even as a poor reader, I could keep up with orchestrations and different things like that. Knowledge of reading music, I do have. And so when Dejon passed out music to read, I was there.
Okay. Yeah. But did you have to work harder once you were in Dejon's band?
To what?
Well, I mean, keep up with the older guys? Keep up with the older guys, yeah.

No, like I say, where I was born, I was born in like a melting pot of musicians. I heard music every day. Live people, the people I mentioned, you know, the Burbanks, the Pernell Brothers, and so many musician families lived in that era where I'm talking about. And it was just the seventh war.
What about schooling? Where did you go to school?
I went to school to Coppus Christi. It was my elementary school, Coppus Christi. And then I went to Joseph S. Clark.
So did you get any music education at- At Clark? No, at Coppus Christi. At Coppus Christi. At grammar school.
Yeah.
Was there any-
I played sticks.
Sticks?

Yeah. Yeah. Just rhythm sticks. Rhythm sticks. Because, well, the kids, we didn't have- We weren't able to have instruments. Only the richer kids could have instruments. They- They- But my family wasn't situated where they could buy me an instrument.
Mm-hmm.
So you had a- They taught us rhythm with sticks, and larger sticks, and some people had a drum and so forth.
So- But this was an organized group?

Well, not so much organized, but it was- If you wanted to be in the organization, or in a group that participated in the players at the school, and the functions, and this, and so forth, and so on. They didn't have instruments, so they gave you what they had.
Mm-hmm.

And you did what you could. You know. We sang in the- In the operata, in the opera, and things like that. Mm-hmm. Because we were being taught- And that's another thing. Our education was taught to us in the 40s like that, in the 30s like that, by Sisters of Blessed Sacrament.
Okay.

And the education was very high. The thing being educated had a very first class in those days. Mm-hmm. And we didn't have- We had very few black teachers in the Catholic school, Archdiocese. Right. So we didn't get black history or anything like that. We had a lot of hand-me-down books from the white schools because that's what the kids got in those days. Mm-hmm. But if you could educate yourself with a good book or a bad book. Right. If you read the book-
Yeah.
You would get something out of it. Yeah. Evidently that's what a lot of us did because a lot of us have achieved greatly from them times.
Yeah.

You know, to what we are today. Some of the leaders of today. So we would read. Music came to me a little bit easier after I went to high school. And that was in 1948, 49 session. Mm-hmm. And this was the beginning of Clark High School.
What-
Pioneer class.
What, the first class you were in there?
First class.
The first-

Well, we were in the first June graduation class. Okay. Because in that, in those days you went to school in January and you went to school in September. Mm-hmm. So you graduated in January or June is the way it was set up.
Mm-hmm.
And it was a platoon system when I first went to school. There was so many, so many kids that had to go to school. We went to school at seven o'clock in the morning.
Oh, at Clark?

Oh, yeah. Okay. It was a, it was down on the main street. It was an old bell school. Mm-hmm. And that was our first school and they moved to Barracks in Robes, Durban in 1950. About 1950 they moved there. So in June of 52 was the first graduating class of Joseph S. Clark. Mm-hmm. You were there? I was in it and I was in the band. In the band we had 65 people.
Well, name, actually the name of all 65. Who?
Well, you can't. Who?
Who? Who? Who? Who? Who was, who was band director? The band, first band director.
The band, first band director was Gordon Garnier. Gordon Garnier. Gordon Garnier was also a local trumpet player with the Dookie Chase Orchestra. Oh, okay.
